name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALDEHYDES_KETONES_AND_CARBOXYLIC_ACIDS_MCQ_Q01 - Hybridisation and geometry change in nucleophilic addition

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates the first step of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl group, showing the attack of a nucleophile on the carbonyl carbon:

Which of the following statements correctly describes the change in hybridisation and geometry of the carbonyl carbon during this process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Diagram and Principle
The diagram depicts the nucleophilic addition mechanism wherein an attacking nucleophile (\(\mathrm{Nu}^-\)) approaches the carbonyl carbon perpendicular to the plane of the carbonyl group.

Step 2: Analysis of the Initial State
In the unreacted carbonyl group (\(>\mathrm{C=O}\)), the carbonyl carbon atom forms three \(\sigma\) bonds and one \(\pi\) bond. The carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised, and the carbonyl carbon along with the three atoms directly bonded to it lie in the same plane with bond angles of approximately \(120^\circ\) (trigonal planar geometry).

Step 3: Transformation During Nucleophilic Attack
As the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, the electron pair of the carbon-oxygen \(\pi\) bond is completely shifted to the electronegative oxygen atom. Consequently, the central carbon forms four single \(\sigma\) bonds (one each to the nucleophile, oxygen, and two substituents).

Step 4: Hybridisation and Geometry of Intermediate
Accommodating four \(\sigma\) bonds requires four equivalent hybrid orbitals, changing the hybridisation of carbon from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\). The spatial arrangement of four equivalent bonds corresponds to a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of approximately \(109.5^\circ\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The process converts a trigonal planar \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbonyl carbon into a tetrahedral \(sp^3\)-hybridised alkoxide intermediate. Therefore, the hybridisation changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\), and the geometry changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral.

answer.text: The hybridisation changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\), and the geometry changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral.
The hybridisation changes from \(sp^3\) to \(sp^2\), and the geometry changes from tetrahedral to trigonal planar.
The hybridisation remains \(sp^2\), while the geometry changes from trigonal planar to T-shaped.
The hybridisation changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp\), and the geometry changes from trigonal planar to linear.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALDEHYDES_KETONES_AND_CARBOXYLIC_ACIDS_MCQ_Q02 - Reaction of phthalic acid with ammonia

questiontext.text:
Consider the reaction sequence shown below starting from benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid (phthalic acid):

What is the structure of the final product [C]?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Scheme and Reagents
The reaction begins with benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid (phthalic acid) reacting with ammonia, followed by stepwise heating to yield intermediate [B] and final product [C].

Step 2: Neutralization to Form Intermediate [A]
Phthalic acid has two acidic carboxyl groups. In the presence of ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)), both carboxyl groups undergo acid-base neutralization to form ammonium phthalate, \(\mathrm{C_6H_4(COONH_4)_2}\), which is intermediate [A].

Step 3: Thermal Dehydration to Form Intermediate [B]
When ammonium phthalate is heated, both ammonium carboxylate moieties lose a molecule of water (\(-2\mathrm{H_2O}\)) to form primary amide groups, producing benzene-1,2-dicarboxamide (commonly known as phthalamide), which is intermediate [B].

Step 4: Strong Heating and Cyclization to Form Product [C]
Upon further strong heating of phthalamide, intramolecular nucleophilic acyl substitution takes place between the adjacent amide groups with the elimination of a molecule of ammonia (\(-\mathrm{NH}_3\)). This generates a stable five-membered ring containing a secondary imide group, giving phthalimide as product [C].

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The loss of ammonia from phthalamide at high temperatures leads specifically to the cyclic imide phthalimide. Thus, the final product [C] is phthalimide.

answer.text: Phthalamide
Phthalimide
Benzamide
Ammonium phthalate

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALDEHYDES_KETONES_AND_CARBOXYLIC_ACIDS_MCQ_Q03 - Cross aldol condensation of benzaldehyde and acetophenone

questiontext.text:
Examine the base-catalyzed condensation reaction presented below:

What is the IUPAC name of the major condensation product [X] formed in this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reactants and Reaction Conditions
The reaction involves benzaldehyde (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)) and acetophenone (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\)) in the presence of dilute sodium hydroxide at \(293\text{ K}\). This is a cross aldol condensation (Claisen-Schmidt reaction).

Step 2: Enolate Generation
Benzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms and cannot undergo enolization. Acetophenone contains three acidic \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms on its methyl group attached to the carbonyl group. The base abstracts an \(\alpha\)-proton from acetophenone to generate the resonance-stabilized enolate ion, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_2^-}\).

Step 3: Nucleophilic Addition and Dehydration
The generated enolate ion attacks the more electrophilic carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde to form a \(\beta\)-hydroxyketone intermediate: \[\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(OH)-CH_2-CO-C_6H_5}\] Because the resulting double bond is conjugated with both the carbonyl group and two aromatic benzene rings, spontaneous dehydration occurs with loss of water to form the \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated ketone: \[\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH=CH-CO-C_6H_5}\]

Step 4: IUPAC Nomenclature
Numbering the three-carbon parent chain from the ketone carbonyl carbon: - Carbon-1 is the carbonyl carbon (\(-\mathrm{CO}-\)) attached to a phenyl substituent. - Carbon-2 and Carbon-3 contain a double bond (\(\text{prop-2-en}\)). - Carbon-3 bears the other phenyl group. This establishes the IUPAC name as 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-one (commonly known as benzalacetophenone).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The major cross aldol condensation product formed between benzaldehyde and acetophenone is 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-one.

answer.text: 1,3-Diphenylpropan-1-one
2,3-Diphenylprop-2-enal
1,3-Diphenylprop-2-en-1-one
3,3-Diphenylprop-2-en-1-one

questiontext.text:
The structure of semicarbazide is shown below with its three nitrogen atoms labeled as 1, 2, and 3:

When semicarbazide reacts with an aldehyde or ketone to form a semicarbazone, which nitrogen atom acts as the nucleophile, and why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Structural Details
Semicarbazide has the formula \(\mathrm{H_2N_{(1)}-C(=O)-NH_{(2)}-NH_{2(3)}}\). It possesses three nitrogen centers: an amide primary nitrogen (1), an amide secondary nitrogen (2), and a hydrazine terminal nitrogen (3).

Step 2: Electronic Delocalization of Nitrogen (1) and (2)
Nitrogen atoms 1 and 2 are directly attached to the strongly electron-withdrawing carbonyl group (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)). Their non-bonding electron pairs participate extensively in resonance with the carbonyl \(\pi\)-system: \[\mathrm{H_2\overset{+}{N}_{(1)}=C(O^-)-NH_{(2)}-NH_{2(3)}}\] Due to this resonance delocalization, the electron density on Nitrogen 1 and Nitrogen 2 is substantially depleted, rendering them poor nucleophiles.

Step 3: Nucleophilic Availability of Nitrogen (3)
Nitrogen 3 is situated at the terminal position of the hydrazine moiety and is separated from the carbonyl group by the \(-\mathrm{NH}-\) group. Its lone pair of electrons is not conjugated with the carbonyl group and remains localized on the nitrogen atom.

Step 4: Formation of Semicarbazone
Because the lone pair on Nitrogen 3 remains freely available, Nitrogen 3 behaves as a potent nucleophile that attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and ketones, followed by dehydration to yield the semicarbazone derivative (\(>\mathrm{C=N-NH-CONH_2}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Nitrogen 3 is the exclusive nucleophilic site because its electron lone pair is localized and not delocalized into the carbonyl group via resonance.

answer.text: Nitrogen 1, because primary amide groups are more basic and less sterically hindered than hydrazine groups.
Nitrogen 2, because secondary amine groups have higher nucleophilicity than primary amine groups.
Both Nitrogen 1 and Nitrogen 3 react with equal probability because both are primary amine groups.
Nitrogen 3, because its lone pair of electrons is not involved in resonance with the carbonyl group, making it significantly more nucleophilic.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALDEHYDES_KETONES_AND_CARBOXYLIC_ACIDS_MCQ_Q05 - Sequential reactions of acetophenone with reagents

questiontext.text:
Acetophenone is subjected to two independent chemical transformations as shown in the roadmap below:

Identify Compound A and Compound B respectively.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reactions
The roadmap shows acetophenone (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\)) undergoing: 1. Reduction using zinc-amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{Zn\text{-}Hg / conc.\ HCl}\)). 2. Oxidation using iodine in sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{I_2 / NaOH}\)) upon heating.

Step 2: Identification of Compound A (Clemmensen Reduction)
Reaction of an aromatic ketone with zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid is the Clemmensen reduction. The carbonyl carbon (\(>\mathrm{C=O}\)) is completely reduced to a methylene group (\(-\mathrm{CH}_2-\)). Consequently, acetophenone (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\)) is transformed into ethylbenzene (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3}\)), which is Compound A.

Step 3: Identification of Compound B (Haloform / Iodoform Reaction)
Acetophenone possesses a methyl group directly linked to a carbonyl carbon (\(\mathrm{-COCH_3}\)). Heating with sodium hypoiodite (\(\mathrm{I_2 / NaOH}\)) causes halogenation of the methyl group followed by carbon-carbon bond cleavage, generating a characteristic yellow precipitate of triiodomethane or iodoform (\(\mathrm{CHI_3}\), Compound B) and the sodium salt of the aromatic acid, sodium benzoate (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}\), Compound C).

Step 4: Check and Plausibility
The molecular structure of Compound A is an 8-carbon alkylarene (ethylbenzene). Compound B is the yellow trihalomethane (iodoform, \(\mathrm{CHI}_3\)).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Compound A is ethylbenzene and Compound B is triiodomethane (iodoform).

answer.text: Compound A is ethylbenzene and Compound B is triiodomethane (iodoform).
Compound A is 1-phenylethanol and Compound B is iodobenzene.
Compound A is ethylbenzene and Compound B is sodium benzoate.
Compound A is toluene and Compound B is triiodomethane (iodoform).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALDEHYDES_KETONES_AND_CARBOXYLIC_ACIDS_MCQ_Q06 - Mechanism and leaving group in esterification

questiontext.text:
The diagram below displays the key tetrahedral intermediates and proton transfer sequence during the acid-catalyzed Fischer esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol:

What is the chemical function of the proton transfer step between Intermediate [I] and Intermediate [II], and what neutral molecule departs as the leaving group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reaction Mechanism
The mechanism depicts acid-catalyzed esterification, which proceeds via nucleophilic acyl substitution on the protonated carboxylic acid by an alcohol (\(\mathrm{R'OH}\)).

Step 2: Nature of Intermediate [I]
Nucleophilic addition of the alcohol yields tetrahedral intermediate [I], \(\mathrm{R-C(OH)_2(\overset{+}{O}H-R')}\). In this species, the hydroxyl groups (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) are strongly basic and constitute poor leaving groups, whereas losing the newly added alcohol would simply revert to starting materials.

Step 3: Purpose of the Proton Transfer
To facilitate forward turnover, a proton transfer occurs from the protonated ether moiety (\(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{O}}\mathrm{HR'}\)) to one of the basic hydroxyl oxygen atoms (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)). This generates intermediate [II] containing a protonated oxonium group (\(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{O}}\mathrm{H}_2\)).

Step 4: Elimination of the Leaving Group
Because water is a very weak conjugate base, \(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{O}}\mathrm{H}_2\) serves as an excellent leaving group. The unshared electron pair of the remaining hydroxyl oxygen atom drives the expulsion of a neutral water molecule (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)), generating the resonance-stabilized protonated ester, which loses a proton to afford the final ester product (\(\mathrm{RCOOR'}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Proton transfer converts the poor leaving hydroxyl group (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) into a good leaving group (\(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{O}}\mathrm{H}_2\)), which is eliminated as a neutral water molecule (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)).

answer.text: Proton transfer converts the alkoxide group into a better leaving group, which departs as a neutral alcohol molecule (\(\mathrm{R'OH}\)).
Proton transfer converts a poor leaving hydroxyl group (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) into a good leaving group (\(-\mathrm{OH}_2^+\)), which departs as a neutral water molecule (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)).
Proton transfer causes deprotonation of the alkyl group, which is eliminated as an alkene.
Proton transfer converts the carboxyl carbon into a carbocation, which eliminates a hydronium ion (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\)).
